meta.topic: The Client and the Agentic Loop
meta.onePayoff: Your app relays between Claude and the server until Claude stops asking for tools — that loop is every MCP application.
meta.openLoop: Claude can't call a tool. So how does a tool ever get called?
meta.analogy: THE PHONE CALL - dial, ask what they can do, ask them to do one, hang up.

seo.title: The MCP Client and the Agentic Loop, Explained Properly
altTitles: Claude Can't Call Tools. Here's What Actually Happens.
The 5 Client Methods And The Loop That Uses Them
seo.hook: Claude never runs your tool. Your code does.
seo.breakdown: the five client methods you actually need, and the relay loop that turns a tool request into an answer

scenes.narration: Here's what confuses everyone at first: Claude can't run your tool. Your own code does.
Once you see the loop that makes that work, the whole protocol clicks — and you'll be able to write the client half yourself. Learn MCP, on THE NBX STUDIO.

scenes.headline: Five methods, [and that's all]
scenes.caption: the phone call
scenes.premise: Connecting is dialling. list_tools is asking what they can do. call_tool is asking them to do one.
scenes.narration: The connection boilerplate never changes between projects, so you write it once and copy it forever. What matters is that there are only five methods you ever need. |List tools asks what can you do, ^and back comes every tool with its description. |Call tool runs one by name, ^and back comes whatever the function returned. |Read resource fetches data your app wants, |list prompts and get prompt handle the user-triggered workflows we met in chapter three. Five methods. That's the entire client surface, and because the connection code around them never changes, there's nothing there worth memorising.

scenes.headline: The loop, [going round]
scenes.caption: the heartbeat
scenes.premise: Your app sits in the middle. Claude is on one side, the MCP server on the other, and your code relays between them.
scenes.narration: Now the part that makes MCP feel alive. Your app runs a loop, and here's one lap of that loop. |Your app loops, and ^you send Claude the user's question together with the tools from the server. ^Claude replies asking for read note with an argument — asking, not doing, and that distinction is the whole reason your app exists. |Then comes the check that ends everything, and we'll come back to that line in a moment. |Your code calls the tool through the client, ^which is the only place in this entire system where anything actually executes. |Then you append the result to the messages list and ^send the whole conversation back to Claude, and round you go again. ^The loop ends when a reply carries no tool request at all, because at that point Claude is answering the person rather than asking your code for something.

lines.detail: The only exit. Not a counter.
Your code executes. Claude never does.
Hand the result back and go round.

scenes.headline: Lap two, and [the answer]
scenes.caption: one question, two tools
scenes.premise: One user question, and Claude needs two different tools before it can answer. Watch the relay go round twice.
scenes.narration: Let's watch a real question go round, because one lap never shows you the point. The user asks: what's on my todo list, and add milk to it. That needs two tools, so it needs two laps. |Lap one, Claude asks to read the note, ^your code runs read note, and the text comes back. |You append that result and send everything back, which means Claude now knows what's on the list. ^Lap two, Claude asks for edit note with milk appended, because Claude can only decide the second step once it has seen the first result. |And on lap three there's no tool request at all — just the sentence for the user — so the loop exits. %Two tool calls, three trips to Claude, and the user typed one line.

lines.detail: Claude asks to read. Your code runs it.
Now Claude knows what's on the list.

scenes.narration: ^The course asks this one, and it's worth getting right. When does the agentic loop stop? ^After exactly three tool calls. ^Or when Claude's reply has no more tool requests in it. Have a think, and pause if you'd like a moment. ^Ready? When there are no more tool requests. There's no counter and no timer — Claude simply stops asking, and a reply with no tool use is Claude talking to the user instead of to your code.

quiz.question: When does the agentic loop stop?
quiz.why: No counter, no timer. Claude just stops asking.

scenes.narration: Three lines to carry. %There are five client methods, and the connection code around them never changes. %Claude asks, and your code is what executes. %And the loop runs until Claude stops asking.
